summary: Carney names a Bridgewater executive to run Canada's new $25-billion wealth fund, the budget sales tour continues, and Ontario teachers keep voting on strikes.
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney named Karen Karniol-Tambour, co-chief investment officer at the US investment firm Bridgewater Associates, as the first CEO of the Canada Strong Fund on Sunday.[^1] The fund is Canada's first national sovereign wealth fund, meaning a government-owned investment pool. It starts with $25 billion, will run at arm's length from the government with its own board, and will invest in big Canadian projects and companies. Ordinary Canadians will be able to buy "Canada Strong Notes" through banks, with their original money protected.[^1]

Carney and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne spent the weekend touring the country to sell last week's budget,[^2] and Carney is in Montreal today to promote its culture funding.[^3] The plan's biggest new item is a $36.1-billion "mega deduction" over five years that lets businesses write off new investments, and the deficit this year is projected at just over $62 billion.[^2] Supporters call it a bet on growth; NDP Leader Avi Lewis says it "doesn't deal with the price of food", and economist Don Drummond says very little of it reaches households.[^2]

Abroad, Canada announced new sanctions on 38 Russian-linked entities and 24 people at the G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris.[^4] For Ontario classrooms, strike votes continue: elementary teachers (ETFO) vote until Nov 18, Catholic teachers on Nov 12-13, and high-school teachers (OSSTF) until Nov 16. A vote passes with more than 50% support, and a "yes" does not mean an immediate strike.[^5]
differences: The government says the budget is about affordability and being "masters of our own destiny"; critics, including the NDP and economist Don Drummond, say most of the money goes to business incentives rather than households.[^2]

reads.title: Carney claims new federal budget will help Canadians with affordability. Experts are divided.
reads.summary: A balanced look at Budget 2026: what is in it, who likes it, and why several economists doubt it will help household costs much.
